title: European markets brace for Fed decision as hot Australia CPI, RBNZ surprise and oil rally stir nerves
summary: It has been quite an eventful start to the day so far as the central bank bonanza rolls into town. That is putting inflation back in the spotlight with there already being plenty to digest before European traders get to their desks and before we even get to the main events later today. To start with, we saw Australia's latest CPI report came in hotter than expected with trimmed mean inflation rising to 3.7%. That's not a good look and RBA governor Bullock was quick to respond in warning that inflation remains "far too high" . The numbers certainly strengthen the argument for another rate hike, with Bullock's response underscoring the narrative that the central bank is facing an increasingly uncomfortable inflation outlook. As such, that is now seeing markets step up their pricing for the next RBA meeting on 3 November, with traders pricing in roughly 76% odds of a 25 bps rate hike. Meanwhile, the RBNZ delivered arguably the bigger surprise of the session after keeping its official cash rate unchanged at 2.75% in a narrow 4-3 vote . Markets had been expecting a 25 bps rate hike today, so the decision has definitely caught traders off guard and sent the kiwi sharply lower. NZD/USD is down 1.1% to 0.5615 on the day currently. Having said that, the central bank hasn't abandoned its tightening bias altogether as the minority continued to take on a more hawkish stance. Bessent says SEC and CFTC can fill the Clarity Act gap, but agency rules come with an expiry risk
summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Washington can still deliver crypto rules without Congress. Speaking at Ripple’s Swell conference, he said the Senate’s failure to pass the Clarity Act was disappointing, but that Treasury would use its convening power to push a regulatory framework forward through agency action with the SEC and CFTC. The catch for investors is durability: rules written by regulators can be rewritten by the next set of regulators. What happened Bessent described the SEC and CFTC as “great partners” in the effort. He also raised debanking, the practice of financial institutions cutting off services to crypto businesses, sometimes allegedly under regulatory pressure. He said the Clarity Act could have prevented a repeat of that, but that regulatory best practices and protections can still reduce the risk. He also argued that stablecoins will lift demand for the US dollar and Treasuries, making them an important funding source for the government. The backdrop is the Senate vote six weeks ago. The Clarity Act failed to advance on September 15 on a 49-50 vote, 11 short of the 60 needed. Because the vote was procedural, the bill was never debated or amended. The two disputes that sank it were ethics rules covering officials’ digital asset holdings and whether stablecoin issuers can offer yield or rewards. title: Australia trimmed mean CPI rises to 3.7%, above forecasts, as RBA hike case firms
summary: Oil is the clearest driver of the headline beat, and Bullock tied higher energy prices directly to a worse inflation outlook only minutes before the release, so any further rise in crude adds to the case for tightening. The bigger signal for markets is the core reading. A trimmed mean that rose to 3.7%, when the RBA had expected it to stabilise, supports pricing for a hike on November 2 and 3, and backs the Australian dollar and front-end yields. The slightly softer weighted median takes a little off that, but not enough to change the overall message. AUD/NZD traders also face the RBNZ decision at 01:00 GMT, where a widely expected hike could limit any relative move in the Aussie. --- Earlier: RBA’s Bullock: oil shock means inflation above August forecasts, Board meets next week --- Australia’s core inflation picked up instead of levelling off, landing just as Governor Bullock was telling senators that inflation is running above the RBA’s forecasts. Summary: Q3 trimmed mean CPI rose 1.0% q/q (expected 1.0%, prior 0.8%) and 3.7% y/y (expected 3.6%, prior 3.6%). Q3 headline CPI rose 1.3% q/q, above the 1.2% forecast and up from 0.6%. September CPI rose 0.8% m/m (expected 0.7%) and 4.3% y/y (expected 4.2%, prior 4.0%). The monthly trimmed mean rose 0.3% m/m and held at 3.6% y/y, both in line with forecasts.
